arXiv:2604.03270v1 [cs.CL] 22 Mar 2026

Knowledge Packs: Zero-Token Knowledge Delivery
via KV Cache Injection

Andrey Pustovit Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: andreyandreevgr@gmail.com
Abstract

RAG wastes tokens. We propose Knowledge Packs: pre-computed KV caches that deliver the same knowledge at zero token cost. For causal transformers, the KV cache from a forward pass on text FF is identical to what a joint pass on F∘qF\circ q would produce—this follows directly from the causal mask. The equivalence is exact but fragile: wrong chat template formatting causes 6–7pp degradation, which we believe explains prior claims of KV outperforming RAG. With correct formatting: zero divergences across 700 questions on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, up to 95% token savings.

The KV interface also enables behavioral steering that RAG cannot do. Because RoPE rotates keys but leaves values untouched, contrastive deltas on cached values can nudge model behavior while key arithmetic destroys coherence. The effect sits in mid-layer values (33–66%), independent directions are nearly orthogonal (cos≈0\cos\approx 0) and compose, and both channels—knowledge and steering—run simultaneously at α≤0.7\alpha{\leq}0.7 without interference. No training, no weight modification.

00footnotetext: Code available at https://github.com/cnails/kv-knowledge-packs

1 Introduction

RAG (Lewis et al., 2020; Guu et al., 2020) solves the knowledge problem by inserting retrieved text into the prompt. One lookup is cheap. But agents that search repeatedly pay a linear tax: 5 searches can consume 700+ tokens on facts alone, eating into the context budget.

We propose Knowledge Packs: pre-computed KV caches that deliver knowledge at zero token cost. In a decoder-only transformer with causal masking, the KV cache from a standalone forward pass on text FF is bit-identical to the KV entries for FF in a joint pass on F∘qF\circ q. We call this KV–Prefix Equivalence. Across 500 HotpotQA questions, KV injection and text-in-prompt produce byte-identical outputs.

Same accuracy, O⁡(1)O(1) token cost instead of O⁡(n)O(n).

The catch is that KV caches must use the model’s chat template. Raw text without special tokens is out-of-distribution for instruction-tuned models and degrades accuracy by 6–7pp. We suspect this is why some prior work reports KV outperforming RAG: the KV and RAG conditions were formatted differently.

There is a second use for KV caches. Contrastive deltas applied to cached values (keys untouched) can steer generation style. At α≤0.5\alpha{\leq}0.5, this works alongside knowledge delivery without interference.

We make four contributions. First, we prove KV–prefix equivalence and verify it empirically (zero divergences across 700 questions on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B), while identifying chat template formatting as a critical pitfall that costs 6–7pp when ignored. Second, we show that KV injection saves up to 95% of tokens in multi-step accumulation and scales to 5,000+ facts via banked routing. Third, we demonstrate that contrastive V-deltas can steer model behavior through KV states that lie outside the image of any token sequence—the effect localizes to mid-layer values and independent directions compose. Fourth, we combine knowledge delivery and value steering in a single cache at α≤0.7\alpha{\leq}0.7.

2 Method

2.1 KV Cache Injection

We pre-compute the KV cache for fact sentences offline and load it as a prefix at inference time.

Write phase (offline, once).

Given fact sentences {f1,…,fn}\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\}, we format them using the model’s chat template as a system message:

Fchat=chat_template(system:f1∘⋯∘fn)F_{\text{chat}}=\texttt{chat\_template}(\texttt{system}:f_{1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{n}) (1)

We tokenize FchatF_{\text{chat}} to obtain 𝐱F=(x1,…,xT)\mathbf{x}_{F}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}) and run a forward pass:

KVF=Model​(𝐱F).past_key_values\text{KV}_{F}=\text{Model}(\mathbf{x}_{F}).\text{past\_key\_values} (2)

producing (𝐊(l),𝐕(l))∈ℝT×dk×ℝT×dv(\mathbf{K}^{(l)},\mathbf{V}^{(l)})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{k}}\times\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{v}} for each layer ll.

Read phase (per query).

Given query qq, we format it as the user message (without system message, since it is already in KV) and generate:

output=Model.generate​(𝐱q,past_key_values=KVF,attention_mask=𝟏T+S)\text{output}=\text{Model.generate}(\mathbf{x}_{q},\;\text{past\_key\_values}=\text{KV}_{F},\;\text{attention\_mask}=\mathbf{1}_{T+S}) (3)

Chat template requirement.

Fact text must be wrapped in the model’s chat template before computing the KV cache. Instruction-tuned models expect special tokens at the start of input (e.g., <|im_start|>system for Qwen). Without them, 7pp degradation on HotpotQA; on structured generation tasks, 0% accuracy.

2.2 KV–Prefix Equivalence Property

Property. For a decoder-only transformer with causal attention, let FF be a fact sequence and qq a query. Then:

KV​(F)⊕generate​(q∣KV​(F))≡generate​(F∘q)\text{KV}(F)\oplus\text{generate}(q\mid\text{KV}(F))\equiv\text{generate}(F\circ q)

That is, pre-computing KV from FF alone and generating qq with that cache produces identical output to generating from the concatenation F∘qF\circ q.

Follows from causal masking: token xix_{i} attends only to j≤ij\leq i, so KV entries at positions 1,…,T1,\ldots,T are the same with or without query tokens appended. Proof by induction on layers in Appendix A. Does not hold for bidirectional or cross-attention.

2.3 Banked Routing

For scaling beyond a single context window, we partition facts into banks via k-means clustering on BGE-large embeddings, with B=⌈N/20⌉B=\lceil N/20\rceil banks. At query time: (1) embed query with BGE, (2) select nearest bank centroid, (3) rank facts within bank, (4) recompute KV for top fact on-the-fly (∼{\sim}5 ms). Storage: <<1 KB/fact (text + embedding), yielding 4 MB for 5,000 facts.

2.4 KV Composition

To compose independently-built caches: process pack A to get KVA\text{KV}_{A}, then process B with KVA\text{KV}_{A} as prefix so that B’s positions continue from TA+1T_{A}{+}1. Simply concatenating two caches does not work—both would start at position 0, breaking RoPE.

3 Experimental Setup

Models.

Two model families, chosen for their different chat template formats:

  • •

    Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025): Primary model, fp16 on NVIDIA A100 80GB. Instruction-tuned with ChatML-style template (<|im_start|>/<|im_end|>).

  • •

    Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey and others, 2024): Secondary model, fp16. Uses a different chat template format (<|start_header_id|>/<|eot_id|>) with auto-injected system preamble (“Cutting Knowledge Date”).

We chose two models specifically because their templates differ—if our results only held for one template format, that would be a problem.

Benchmarks.

  • •

    HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018): Multi-hop QA with 2 gold + 8 distractor paragraphs per question. N=500N{=}500 (Qwen) and N=200N{=}200 (Llama) from the dev set (75% bridge + 25% comparison).

  • •

    HotpotQA Accumulation: Same question pool with 1–5 sequential retrieval steps, measuring how token cost scales. N=100N{=}100 per level per model.

  • •

    Value Steering: 15 coding tasks scored for defensive patterns (0–9 scale), tested with 30 contrastive code example pairs (“good”: defensive, error-handling vs. “bad”: sloppy, no checks). Both models.

  • •

    Dual-Channel: 200 HotpotQA bridge questions with simultaneous knowledge KV and formality V-delta, measuring both factual EM and behavioral effect. Qwen3-8B.

Methods compared.

  • •

    Baseline: No external knowledge.

  • •

    RAG: Retrieved paragraphs in system message via chat template.

  • •

    KV-chat: Same paragraphs as KV cache, built with chat template (same system message as RAG). Identical text and formatting; only the delivery mechanism differs.

  • •

    KV-raw: Same paragraphs as KV cache, built from raw text without chat template. Included to quantify the chat template effect.

This is important: RAG and KV-chat use identical system messages, character for character. The only variable is whether the text arrives via prompt or via pre-computed cache. Without this control, formatting differences alone can produce 5–10pp gaps, as we show in Section 4.3.

Retrieval.

BGE-large-en-v1.5 (Xiao et al., 2023) top-2 retrieval from all 10 paragraphs.

Evaluation.

Exact match (gold answer substring in prediction) and token-overlap F1.

4 Results

4.1 HotpotQA: KV = RAG at Zero Token Cost

Table 1 has the main result.

Zero divergences across 700 comparisons. Qwen: 326 both correct, 174 both wrong, 0 disagreements. Llama: 123/77/0. Byte-identical outputs.

KV-raw (no chat template) costs 6.0pp on Qwen, 5.5pp on Llama. The damage concentrates on bridge questions (6.4pp and 7.4pp); comparison questions are barely affected, probably because single-fact lookups are more robust to formatting noise. If the KV and RAG conditions in a study use different formatting, this alone can account for reported accuracy gaps.

4.2 Accumulation Scaling: Constant vs. Linear Token Cost

Table 2 shows multi-step retrieval, where an agent accumulates facts over sequential searches.

Equivalence holds at every level (one 1pp discrepancy at N=100N{=}100, noise). Accuracy plateaus around 3 steps.

RAG adds roughly 140–150 tokens per step; KV stays at 31–35 (just the question). At 5 steps this means ∼{\sim}700 tokens saved per query. In a 32K context window with average paragraph length of 150 tokens, RAG would hit the context limit at around 200 accumulated facts. KV has no such ceiling.

4.3 Chat Template Analysis

Why does some prior work report KV >> RAG?

The gap is 5.5–6.0pp overall, concentrated on bridge questions where the model needs to cross-reference multiple facts.

Template split pitfall.

A subtler problem: calling apply_chat_template separately for system and user parts can insert duplicate special tokens. On Llama-3.1 this re-adds <|begin_of_text|> and an empty system header, which costs another 1.5pp. The fix is to generate the full template (system+user) in one call and split at the boundary. Qwen’s template does not have this problem.

These two pitfalls together can shift accuracy by 5–10pp. To be safe, verify that the concatenated KV+prompt token sequence is byte-identical to the single-pass RAG sequence before drawing any conclusions.

4.4 Scaling with Banked Routing

We evaluate KV injection at increasing fact counts using synthetic facts with Qwen3-8B (Table 4).

Routing accuracy: 100% at all scales. Storage grows linearly at <<1 KB/fact.

4.5 KV Composition

Table 5 tests whether independently-built KV caches can be composed.

They can. Naive concatenation loses 6pp (both caches start at RoPE position 0), but sequential composition—running B with KVA\text{KV}_{A} as prefix—preserves accuracy.

4.6 Beyond Equivalence: Value-Space Steering

Everything above is lossless optimization—same outputs, fewer tokens. But KV caches also give us write access to the model’s internal state. What if we write something that no text could produce?

We initially tried arithmetic on both keys and values. Keys broke immediately: coherence dropped to 27% at α=1.0\alpha{=}1.0. This makes sense once you look at how RoPE (Su et al., 2024) works—keys are rotated by position (𝐤i=Rθ​(i)⋅WK​𝐱i\mathbf{k}_{i}=R_{\theta}(i)\cdot W_{K}\mathbf{x}_{i}), and adding rotated vectors from different positions produces garbage. Values are not rotated (𝐯i=WV​𝐱i\mathbf{v}_{i}=W_{V}\mathbf{x}_{i}). They tolerate arithmetic.

So we tried value-only steering. We construct matched pairs of code examples (“good”: defensive, error-handling vs. “bad”: no validation, common pitfalls), keeping structure and variable names identical across pairs. From these we build KVgood\text{KV}_{\text{good}} and KVbad\text{KV}_{\text{bad}} and steer a fresh base cache:

𝐕steered(l)=𝐕base(l)+α⋅(𝐕good(l)−𝐕bad(l)),𝐊steered(l)=𝐊base(l)\mathbf{V}^{(l)}_{\text{steered}}=\mathbf{V}^{(l)}_{\text{base}}+\alpha\cdot(\mathbf{V}^{(l)}_{\text{good}}-\mathbf{V}^{(l)}_{\text{bad}}),\quad\mathbf{K}^{(l)}_{\text{steered}}=\mathbf{K}^{(l)}_{\text{base}} (4)

Keys are left alone. This is activation steering (Turner et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024a) applied to cached values instead of hidden states.

Table 6 sweeps α\alpha. Score is defensive coding quality (0–9, 15 tasks, pattern-matched); coherence is fraction of syntactically valid outputs.

Optimal α\alpha: 2.0 for Qwen (0.60→\to1.93), 1.5 for Llama (1.47→\to2.47). Text-in-prompt scores 3.67 and 3.80 respectively, so this is about half as strong. Qwen is fragile—collapses at α=3.0\alpha{=}3.0 (20% coherence). Llama is more forgiving, still coherent at 3.0.

Table 7 breaks this down by layer.

Mid layers (33–66%) carry the full effect on Qwen (1.93 = all-layer score) and 92% on Llama. Late layers do nothing—0.67 on Qwen where baseline is 0.60, and literally 1.47 = 1.47 on Llama.

This is a strong result. It means we can apply steering to only 12 of 36 layers and lose nothing. It also means something about where “style” lives in these models, though we will not speculate further here.

5 contrastive pairs and 30 give the same score (1.13 at α=1.0\alpha{=}1.0). The direction saturates fast. Oddly, text-in-prompt gets worse with more examples (4.13→\to3.67).

We also tested composition (Table 8):

𝐕steered=𝐕base+∑iαi⋅Δ​𝐕i,𝐊steered=𝐊base\mathbf{V}_{\text{steered}}=\mathbf{V}_{\text{base}}+\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{V}_{i},\quad\mathbf{K}_{\text{steered}}=\mathbf{K}_{\text{base}} (5)

We test two directions: “defensive coding” (Δ​𝐕A\Delta\mathbf{V}_{A}: error handling, type checks) and “documentation” (Δ​𝐕B\Delta\mathbf{V}_{B}: docstrings, type hints, comments). The cosine similarity between them is 0.0003±0.0120.0003\pm 0.012, i.e., they are nearly orthogonal.

A+B together is better than either alone: 131%/89% retention on Qwen, 114%/115% on Llama. The deltas are nearly orthogonal (cos=0.0003\cos{=}0.0003 on Qwen, cos=0.040\cos{=}0.040 on Llama), which explains why they compose without interference.

𝐕base+∑iαi⋅Δ​𝐕i\mathbf{V}_{\text{base}}+\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{V}_{i} is not in the image of any token sequence—no text produces this KV state. Everything in this subsection (mid-layer localization, composability, near-orthogonality) replicates on both Qwen and Llama.

4.7 Dual-Channel Architecture: Knowledge + Steering

Can we do both at once—knowledge via full KV, steering via mid-layer V-delta? 200 HotpotQA bridge questions, Qwen3-8B, gold paragraphs as knowledge, “formal/detailed” V-delta. Six conditions in Table 9.

At α=2.0\alpha{=}2.0 (the steering-only optimum), accuracy drops from 72.5% to 40.5%. Too much. Table 10 sweeps lower values.

α≤0.7\alpha{\leq}0.7: 72–73% EM (same as knowledge-only), formality up 20%, responses 45 vs. 35 words. No accuracy cost. At 1.0 accuracy starts to slip (67%). Past 1.5, steering dominates (55%).

We think this works because the two channels occupy different parts of the KV space. Knowledge spans all layers, both K and V. Steering only touches mid-layer V. At moderate α\alpha they mostly do not overlap.

5 Analysis and Discussion

KV = RAG is not a negative result. It is a lossless optimization: swap in a cache, get the same outputs, no tuning. The use cases are pay-per-token APIs, long conversations, agentic workflows. Build cost is ∼{\sim}5ms/fact. The main downside is that a Llama cache will not load into Qwen—KV caches are tied to a specific architecture, unlike RAG text.

Chat template as distribution shift.

This one surprised us. Both model families lose 6–7pp with raw-text KV, even though their template formats are completely different (ChatML vs. Llama-style headers). Our best explanation is that the special tokens act as mode switches: <|im_start|>system tells Qwen “what follows is instructions,” and without it the model processes the same text differently. The degradation is worst on bridge questions, where the model must cross-reference two passages—single-fact comparison questions are barely affected. We spent a while debugging this before realizing the template was the issue, and we suspect others have hit the same problem without identifying the cause.

This connects to a broader point about prior work claiming KV >> RAG. We found three confounds that can produce this: (1) raw-text KV (−-6pp), (2) duplicate BOS from template splitting (−-1.5pp on Llama), (3) different system prompt content between conditions. Any one of them can flip the comparison.

6 Related Work

RAG.

Lewis et al. (2020); Guu et al. (2020), with multi-hop extensions (Trivedi et al., 2023; Press et al., 2023; Asai et al., 2024). KV injection replaces the prompt-insertion step.

KV cache compression and serving.

H2O (Zhang et al., 2023), ScissorHands (Liu et al., 2024), SnapKV (Li et al., 2024b) prune cache entries; these could be applied on top of our method. Prefix caching in vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) shares KV for common prefixes. Shkolnikov (2026) study persistent KV caches for multi-agent settings. We add the equivalence proof and the chat template requirement, which none of these works address.

Prompt and prefix tuning.

Prefix tuning (Li and Liang, 2021) and prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021) prepend learned representations but require training. Our caches come from natural language.

Activation steering.

This is the closest line of work to our value steering. Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al., 2024a) compute steering vectors from contrastive pairs and add them to hidden states during the forward pass. We do the same thing, but on cached values rather than live activations, which means the steering is applied once at cache construction time and costs nothing at inference. The key difference is that we cannot touch keys (RoPE makes key arithmetic destructive), so we are limited to the value subspace. Whether this is a fundamental limitation or just a property of RoPE architectures is unclear.

Knowledge editing.

ROME (Meng et al., 2022), MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023). Weight editing. We do not modify weights.

7 Conclusion

Pre-computed KV caches are a lossless, zero-token replacement for RAG prompt insertion. Zero divergences on 700 questions, two models, up to 95% token savings at 5 retrieval steps. The main practical requirement is correct chat template formatting.

Separately, the RoPE K/V asymmetry opens up value-space steering: contrastive V-deltas applied to mid layers can nudge model behavior without re-running inference, and independent directions compose. Both channels—knowledge and steering—run simultaneously at α≤0.7\alpha{\leq}0.7 without degrading either.

Limitations.

The most obvious limitation is that KV caches do not transfer across models. Value steering, while consistent, only reaches about half the effect of text-in-prompt (1.93–2.47 vs. 3.67–3.80 on our coding tasks). We also have limited scale: 15 coding tasks for steering, 200 questions for dual-channel, and steering was only tested on coding style—we do not know if it transfers to, say, tone or factuality. The routing evaluation used synthetic facts that are easy to distinguish; real knowledge bases would be harder. Finally, α\alpha must be reduced in dual-channel mode compared to steering-only, which tells us the two subspaces are not fully orthogonal despite what the cosine similarities suggest.

Appendix A Proof of KV–Prefix Equivalence

Claim. KVF(l)=KVF∘q(l)[1:T]\text{KV}^{(l)}_{F}=\text{KV}^{(l)}_{F\circ q}[1{:}T] for all layers ll.

The argument is simple. Causal mask: position ii sees only j≤ij\leq i. So appending qq after position TT cannot affect KV entries at positions 1,…,T1,\ldots,T. This holds at layer 1 (embeddings depend only on token identity and position), and propagates by induction—layer ll at position i≤Ti\leq T depends only on layer l−1l{-}1 outputs at positions ≤i\leq i, all of which are identical by hypothesis. Given identical caches, generation from T+1T{+}1 is deterministic and identical. □\square

Requires causal masking, position encodings that depend on index only, deterministic decoding.

Appendix B Synthetic Scaling Tests

Scaling evaluation with Qwen3-8B using fictional facts:

  • •

    Single KV cache: 100% accuracy at 1,000 facts (8,434 tokens).

  • •

    Banked KV: 100% routing and answer accuracy at 5,000 facts with 250 banks.

  • •

    Lazy recompute: 4.2 MB storage, 6 ms per-query overhead.
